questions.prompt: Which food molecule is given as the example that is broken down in respiration?
questions.explanation: Food molecules such as glucose are broken down during respiration to release energy.

questions.prompt: Which gas is required for the complete oxidation of food in aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: In aerobic respiration, oxygen is required for the complete oxidation of food molecules.

questions.prompt: Which gas is released as a by-product of aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: In aerobic respiration, carbon dioxide is released as a by-product.

questions.prompt: Oxygen is released as a by-product of which process?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released as a by-product of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What is the ultimate source of energy for life?
questions.explanation: The ultimate source of energy for life is sunlight.

questions.prompt: Organisms take oxygen from the environment, which can be air or what else?
questions.explanation: All organisms take oxygen from the environment (air or water) and release carbon dioxide into it.

questions.prompt: Which gases are exchanged between an organism and its environment in gaseous exchange?
questions.explanation: Gaseous exchange is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment.

questions.prompt: By which process does gaseous exchange occur?
questions.explanation: Gaseous exchange occurs by diffusion.

questions.prompt: In diffusion, molecules move from a region of which concentration to a region of lower concentration?
questions.explanation: Diffusion is a process in which molecules move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

questions.prompt: Breathing is which kind of process?
questions.explanation: Breathing is the physical process in which animals move air into and out of their body.

questions.prompt: Animals breathe to get which gas from the air?
questions.explanation: Animals breathe to get oxygen from air and to release carbon dioxide in it.

questions.prompt: In breathing, fresh air is made available to the respiratory surface of which organ?
questions.explanation: In breathing, fresh air is made available to the respiratory surface of the lung for gaseous exchange.

questions.prompt: Compared with the blood, what is the oxygen concentration of fresh air in the lungs?
questions.explanation: Fresh air has a higher concentration of oxygen than the blood, so oxygen diffuses into the blood.

questions.prompt: Which process is the chemical, energy-releasing process inside cells?
questions.explanation: Cellular respiration is a chemical, energy-releasing process inside cells, whereas breathing is only the physical movement of air.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.1, in which process is oxygen used to oxidise food and carbon dioxide produced?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is used to oxidise food and carbon dioxide is produced during cellular respiration.

questions.prompt: Respiration at the cellular level is known as:
questions.explanation: At the cellular level, respiration is the oxidation of food molecules with the release of energy.

questions.prompt: Which process do the green parts of a plant carry out, in addition to respiration, during the daytime?
questions.explanation: During the daytime, all plant cells carry out respiration, while the green parts also carry out photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Leaves use the carbon dioxide produced during which process for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: For photosynthesis, leaves use the carbon dioxide produced during respiration and also take carbon dioxide from the environment.

questions.prompt: Leaves use the oxygen produced during which process for respiration?
questions.explanation: For respiration, leaves use the oxygen produced during photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which gas do leaves take in from the environment during the daytime?
questions.explanation: During the daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide from the environment and release oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which gas do leaves release into the environment during the daytime?
questions.explanation: During the daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide from the environment and release oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which gas do plant cells take in from the environment at night?
questions.explanation: At night, plant cells take in oxygen from the environment.

questions.prompt: Which gas do plant cells release into the environment at night?
questions.explanation: At night, plant cells release carbon dioxide into the environment.

questions.prompt: Which process do all plant cells carry out at night?
questions.explanation: At night all plant cells carry out respiration.

questions.prompt: What is the outer surface of the root, stem and leaves called?
questions.explanation: The outer surface of the root, stem and leaves is called the epidermis.

questions.prompt: Through which structures does air move in and out in leaves and young stems?
questions.explanation: In leaves and young stems, air moves in and out through the stomata.

questions.prompt: Stomata are present in the epidermis of leaves and which other plant part?
questions.explanation: Stomata are present in the epidermis of leaves and young stems.

questions.prompt: What are the special pores in the bark of woody stems called?
questions.explanation: The special pores in the bark of woody stems are called lenticels.

questions.prompt: What covers the entire surface of woody stems?
questions.explanation: In woody stems, the entire surface is covered by bark.

questions.prompt: Through which structure of woody stems can gaseous exchange not occur?
questions.explanation: Gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark.

questions.prompt: Lenticels allow gaseous exchange in which kind of stems?
questions.explanation: Lenticels allow gaseous exchange in woody stems.

questions.prompt: What does a large surface area allow, for the amount of gas diffusing in and out at the same time?
questions.explanation: A large surface area allows more gas to diffuse in and out at the same time.

questions.prompt: Tilling helps soil drainage and which other property?
questions.explanation: Farmers and gardeners till the soil, which helps soil drainage and aeration.

questions.prompt: Air spaces in tilled soil allow better gas exchange between the air and which plant part?
questions.explanation: The air spaces in tilled soil allow better exchange of gases between the roots and the air.

questions.prompt: Which part, besides the cuticle and mesophyll, is labelled in the leaf diagram of Fig. 10.2 (b)?
questions.explanation: In the gaseous exchange diagram of a leaf (Fig. 10.2 b), the labelled parts are the cuticle, mesophyll and stoma.

questions.prompt: What does Fig. 10.3 show in a bark?
questions.explanation: Fig. 10.3 shows lenticels in a bark.

questions.prompt: In the bicarbonate indicator activity, which colour shows that the carbon dioxide level has increased?
questions.explanation: In the bicarbonate indicator activity, the indicator turns yellow when the carbon dioxide level increases.

questions.prompt: In the bicarbonate indicator activity, which colour shows that the carbon dioxide level has decreased?
questions.explanation: In the bicarbonate indicator activity, the indicator turns purple when the carbon dioxide level decreases.

questions.prompt: What is the colour of the bicarbonate indicator at the normal carbon dioxide level?
questions.explanation: The bicarbonate indicator is red at the normal carbon dioxide level.

questions.prompt: A leaf is kept in the dark in a tube of bicarbonate indicator. What colour does the indicator turn?
questions.explanation: A leaf kept in the dark in a tube of bicarbonate indicator turns the indicator yellow because only respiration occurs and carbon dioxide is released.

questions.prompt: In the bicarbonate indicator activity, what is the tube without a leaf called?
questions.explanation: In the leaf activity, a tube without a leaf is kept as a control.

questions.prompt: What happens to clear lime water when exhaled air is blown through it?
questions.explanation: When exhaled air is blown through clear lime water, the lime water turns milky.

questions.prompt: Exhaled air turns lime water milky because it contains which gas?
questions.explanation: Exhaled air turns lime water milky because it contains carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: In the breathing-rate activity, what is counted for one minute?
questions.explanation: To find the breathing rate, count the number of breaths in one minute.

questions.prompt: What is the collective name of the connected tubes through which air reaches the lungs?
questions.explanation: The connected tubes through which air reaches the lungs are collectively called the air passageway.

questions.prompt: The human respiratory system consists of the air passageway and which other component?
questions.explanation: The human respiratory system can be divided into the air passageway and the lungs.

questions.prompt: For which mode of life is the human respiratory system well adapted?
questions.explanation: The human respiratory system is well adapted for the terrestrial mode of life.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the last tube listed in the air passageway after the bronchi?
questions.explanation: The air passageway consists of the nostrils and nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.

questions.prompt: How many external nostril openings are present on the ventral side of the head?
questions.explanation: The external nostrils are two openings on the ventral side of the head.

questions.prompt: On which side of the head are the external nostrils present?
questions.explanation: The external nostrils are openings on the ventral side of the head.

questions.prompt: The external nostrils allow outside air to enter which structures?
questions.explanation: The external nostrils allow air from outside into the two nasal cavities.

questions.prompt: In the nasal cavities, air is warmed, moistened and freed from what?
questions.explanation: In the nasal cavities, air is warmed, moistened and freed from dust.

questions.prompt: Which structures of the nasal cavity, along with the mucous membrane, free the air from dust?
questions.explanation: In the nasal cavities, dust is removed from the air by the hairs and the mucous membrane.

questions.prompt: Through which organ should we breathe to keep ourselves healthy?
questions.explanation: We should breathe through the nose and not through the mouth to keep ourselves healthy.

questions.prompt: Which muscular passage, about 4.5 inches long, receives air from the nasal cavities?
questions.explanation: The pharynx is a muscular passage about 4.5 inches long into which the nasal cavities lead.

questions.prompt: About how long is the pharynx?
questions.explanation: The pharynx is about 4.5 inches long.

questions.prompt: The tonsils and adenoids are organs of which type of tissue?
questions.explanation: The tonsils and adenoids in the pharynx are organs of lymphatic tissue.

questions.prompt: What do the tonsils and adenoids trap and filter?
questions.explanation: The tonsils and adenoids trap and filter microorganisms.

questions.prompt: In which part of the air passageway are the tonsils and adenoids found?
questions.explanation: The tonsils and adenoids are found in the pharynx.

questions.prompt: At the back of the pharynx, the glottis opens into which tube?
questions.explanation: At the back of the pharynx, one passage opens into the esophagus and the other opens through the glottis into the trachea.

questions.prompt: On which side does the passage from the back of the pharynx open into the esophagus?
questions.explanation: At the back of the pharynx, one passage opens into the esophagus on the dorsal side.

questions.prompt: On which side of the pharynx does the glottis lead into the trachea?
questions.explanation: The glottis leads into the trachea on the ventral side.

questions.prompt: What is the opening that leads from the back of the pharynx into the trachea called?
questions.explanation: The opening through which air passes into the trachea is called the glottis.

questions.prompt: What does the epiglottis prevent from entering the larynx?
questions.explanation: The epiglottis prevents food from entering the larynx.

questions.prompt: Which part of the air passageway is also called the voice box?
questions.explanation: The voice box is the larynx.

questions.prompt: From which part does air move into the larynx?
questions.explanation: Air moves into the larynx from the pharynx.

questions.prompt: The larynx surrounds the upper part of which tube?
questions.explanation: The larynx surrounds the upper part of the trachea.

questions.prompt: The cavity of the larynx is lined by which kind of membrane?
questions.explanation: The cavity of the larynx is lined by a mucous membrane.

questions.prompt: Which part of the air passageway is also called the windpipe?
questions.explanation: The wind pipe is the trachea.

questions.prompt: Relative to the esophagus, on which side does the trachea lie?
questions.explanation: The trachea lies ventral to the esophagus.

questions.prompt: The trachea extends to the chest cavity. What is the chest cavity also called?
questions.explanation: The trachea extends to the chest cavity, which is also called the thorax.

questions.prompt: Which feature describes the inner surface of the trachea, which also secretes mucus?
questions.explanation: The inner surface of the trachea is ciliated and secretes mucus.

questions.prompt: What does the inner surface of the trachea secrete to filter, moisten and warm the incoming air?
questions.explanation: The inner surface of the trachea secretes mucus, which helps to filter, moisten and warm the incoming air.

questions.prompt: How many C-shaped cartilaginous rings does the trachea have?
questions.explanation: The trachea has 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of the cartilaginous rings of the trachea?
questions.explanation: The cartilaginous rings of the trachea are C-shaped.

questions.prompt: The cartilaginous rings keep the air passage open by preventing the trachea from:
questions.explanation: The cartilaginous rings prevent the trachea from collapsing and keep the air passage open.

questions.prompt: Compared with those of the trachea, how are the cartilaginous rings of the bronchi?
questions.explanation: The cartilaginous rings of the bronchi are smaller than those of the trachea.

questions.prompt: What are the smaller bronchi of 1 mm diameter or less called?
questions.explanation: Smaller bronchi of 1 mm diameter or less are called bronchioles.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum diameter of a bronchiole?
questions.explanation: Bronchioles have a diameter of 1 mm or less.

questions.prompt: Each bronchiole ends in a duct that opens in a cluster of:
questions.explanation: Each bronchiole ends in a duct that opens in a cluster of alveoli.

questions.prompt: What is an alveolus?
questions.explanation: An alveolus is a microscopic, thin-walled pouch at the end of a bronchiole.

questions.prompt: The alveoli resemble bunches of which fruit?
questions.explanation: The alveoli resemble bunches of grapes.

questions.prompt: The alveoli provide the surface for which process?
questions.explanation: The alveoli provide the surface for gaseous exchange.

questions.prompt: The walls of the alveoli are covered with a network of which vessels?
questions.explanation: The walls of the alveoli are covered with a network of blood capillaries.

questions.prompt: Which feature of the alveolar wall makes the alveoli an excellent site for gaseous exchange?
questions.explanation: The alveoli are very thin-walled, which makes them an excellent site for gaseous exchange.

questions.prompt: Which part follows the pharynx in the path of air?
questions.explanation: In the path of air, the pharynx is followed by the larynx.

questions.prompt: Into which tubes does the trachea divide in the path of air?
questions.explanation: In the path of air, the trachea divides into the bronchi.

questions.prompt: The bronchi sub-divide and lead to which tubes?
questions.explanation: In the path of air, the bronchi sub-divide and lead to the bronchioles.

questions.prompt: In the path of air, the bronchioles end in clusters of:
questions.explanation: In the path of air, the bronchioles end in clusters of alveoli.

questions.prompt: Through which structures does air first enter the body?
questions.explanation: The part of the air passageway through which air first enters the body is the external nostrils.

questions.prompt: After gaseous exchange, how does air move from the lungs to the outside?
questions.explanation: After gaseous exchange, air moves from the lungs to the outside through the same connected tubes.

options: Through a different set of tubes

questions.prompt: Air passes through the larynx before reaching which tube, which divides into the bronchi?
questions.explanation: Air passes through the larynx before reaching the trachea, which divides into the bronchi.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a part of the air passageway?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is not a part of the air passageway.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a function of the nasal cavities?
questions.explanation: Producing the voice is not a function of the nasal cavities, which warm, moisten and free the air from dust.

questions.prompt: From above and the sides, what encloses the lungs?
questions.explanation: From above and the sides, the lungs are enclosed by the chest wall.

questions.prompt: Which thick muscular structure lies below the lungs?
questions.explanation: Below the lungs there is a thick muscular structure called the diaphragm.

questions.prompt: What is the double membrane that encloses each lung called?
questions.explanation: Each lung is enclosed in a double membrane called the pleura.

questions.prompt: What is the fluid present in the pleura called?
questions.explanation: The fluid present in the pleura is called the pleural fluid.

questions.prompt: The pleural fluid makes which movements of the lungs easy: expansion and what?
questions.explanation: The pleural fluid makes the movements of the lungs, i.e. expansion and contraction, easy.

questions.prompt: The size of the lungs of an organism is related to its activities and what else?
questions.explanation: The size of the lungs of an organism is related to its activities and body form.

questions.prompt: What can be said about the lungs of a cheetah and an elephant?
questions.explanation: The cheetah and the elephant have large lungs.

questions.prompt: Which sinuses are labelled in Fig. 10.5?
questions.explanation: The sinuses labelled in the general outline of the respiratory system (Fig. 10.5) are the ethmoid sinuses.

questions.prompt: Which structure, along with the pleural cavity and both lungs, is labelled in Fig. 10.4?
questions.explanation: Fig. 10.4 shows the pleural cavity, right lung, left lung and the diaphragm.

questions.prompt: What is the taking in of air called?
questions.explanation: The taking in of air is called inspiration.

questions.prompt: What is the letting out of air called?
questions.explanation: The letting out of air is called expiration.

questions.prompt: Air moves into the lungs when the pressure in the lungs is ____ than the pressure outside the body.
questions.explanation: Air moves into the lungs when the air pressure in the lungs is lower than the pressure outside the body.

questions.prompt: Air moves out of the lungs when the pressure in the lungs is ____ than the atmospheric pressure.
questions.explanation: Air moves out of the lungs when the pressure in the lungs is greater than the atmospheric pressure.

questions.prompt: Which structure bounds the thorax on the ventral side?
questions.explanation: The thorax is bound by the sternum on the ventral side.

questions.prompt: Which structure bounds the thorax on the dorsal side?
questions.explanation: The thorax is bound by the backbone on the dorsal side.

questions.prompt: Which structure bounds the thorax at the posterior end?
questions.explanation: The thorax is bound by the diaphragm at the posterior end.

questions.prompt: What is the sternum?
questions.explanation: The sternum is the chest bone.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of the diaphragm at rest?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscles.

questions.prompt: The diaphragm is a sheet of which type of muscles?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a sheet of skeletal muscles.

questions.prompt: The diaphragm separates the chest cavity from which cavity?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity.

questions.prompt: What are the muscles in between the ribs called?
questions.explanation: The muscles in between the ribs are called intercostal muscles.

questions.prompt: What happens to the muscles of the diaphragm during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the muscles of the diaphragm contract.

questions.prompt: What shape does the diaphragm take during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the diaphragm becomes flat instead of dome-shaped.

questions.prompt: What happens to the intercostal muscles during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract.

questions.prompt: What happens to the pressure in the lungs during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the pressure in the lungs decreases.

questions.prompt: What happens to the muscles of the ribs and the diaphragm during expiration?
questions.explanation: During expiration, the muscles of the ribs and the diaphragm relax.

questions.prompt: What shape does the diaphragm take during expiration?
questions.explanation: During expiration, the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped.

questions.prompt: In which direction does the ribcage move during expiration?
questions.explanation: During expiration, the ribcage goes down to its original position.

questions.prompt: What happens to the volume of the chest cavity during expiration?
questions.explanation: During expiration, the volume of the chest cavity decreases.

questions.prompt: What happens to the air in the lungs during expiration?
questions.explanation: During expiration, air is expelled from the lungs.

questions.prompt: In which direction does the diaphragm move during inhalation (Fig. 10.6)?
questions.explanation: In Fig. 10.6, the diaphragm moves down during inhalation.

questions.prompt: In which direction does the diaphragm move during exhalation (Fig. 10.6)?
questions.explanation: In Fig. 10.6, the diaphragm moves up during exhalation.

questions.prompt: The diaphragm is flat and the ribs move out. This occurs during:
questions.explanation: When the diaphragm is flat and the ribs move out, the person is in the phase of inspiration.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.6, what do the rib muscles do while the rib cage gets smaller?
questions.explanation: In Fig. 10.6, the rib cage gets smaller as the rib muscles relax during exhalation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an event of expiration?
questions.explanation: Pressure on the lungs decreases is not an event of expiration; there the pressure increases.

questions.prompt: Oxygen from the alveoli diffuses into which vessels?
questions.explanation: Oxygen from the alveoli diffuses into the blood capillaries.

questions.prompt: How is the oxygen concentration of the blood that enters the capillaries around the alveoli?
questions.explanation: The blood entering the capillaries around the alveoli has a low oxygen concentration.

questions.prompt: Compared with the blood entering the capillaries, how is the oxygen concentration of the inhaled air in the alveoli?
questions.explanation: The inhaled air present in the alveoli has a higher oxygen concentration than the blood entering the capillaries.

questions.prompt: Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood of the capillaries and into which structures?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood and into the alveoli.

questions.prompt: By which process do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveoli?
questions.explanation: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveoli by diffusion.

questions.prompt: Through which vessel does deoxygenated blood reach the capillaries around an alveolus (Fig. 10.7)?
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood reaches the capillaries around an alveolus through an arteriole.

questions.prompt: Through which vessel does oxygenated blood return from an alveolus (Fig. 10.7)?
questions.explanation: After gaseous exchange, oxygenated blood returns from the alveolus through a venule.

questions.prompt: Oxygen from the lungs enters into the blood due to:
questions.explanation: Oxygen from the lungs enters into the blood due to diffusion.

options: Less affinity of O₂ for air
Higher affinity of CO₂ for air

questions.prompt: Expired air has more carbon dioxide because carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into which structures?
questions.explanation: The air breathed out has more carbon dioxide because carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

questions.prompt: What is the rate of breathing, in times per minute, under resting conditions?
questions.explanation: Under resting conditions, the rate of breathing is 15–20 times per minute.

questions.prompt: Up to how many times per minute does the breathing rate rise during exercise?
questions.explanation: During exercise, the rate of breathing increases up to 30–40 times per minute.

questions.prompt: What happens to the rate of breathing during exercise?
questions.explanation: During exercise, the rate of breathing increases instantly.

questions.prompt: During exercise, more of which gas is required for the oxidation of glucose to get more energy?
questions.explanation: During exercise, more oxygen is required for the oxidation of glucose molecules to get more energy.

questions.prompt: Where does the extra carbon dioxide produced during exercise accumulate?
questions.explanation: During exercise, more carbon dioxide is produced, which accumulates in the blood.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is the breathing centre?
questions.explanation: The medulla of the brain is the breathing centre.

questions.prompt: What does the medulla detect in increased amounts in the blood during exercise?
questions.explanation: During exercise, the medulla detects more carbon dioxide in the blood.

questions.prompt: To which muscles does the medulla send nerve impulses at greater speed during exercise: rib muscles and the:
questions.explanation: During exercise, the medulla sends nerve impulses to the diaphragm and rib muscles at greater speed.

questions.prompt: What happens to the speed of contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and rib muscles during exercise?
questions.explanation: During exercise, the speed of contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and rib muscles increases.

questions.prompt: During exercise, both the rate and which other feature of breathing increase?
questions.explanation: During exercise, the increased nerve impulses raise both the rate and the depth of breathing.

questions.prompt: Why is a morning walk beneficial for gaseous exchange? It increases the rate and depth of:
questions.explanation: Walking in the morning increases the rate and depth of breathing, so more oxygen is taken into the blood.

questions.prompt: Compared with the breathing rate during exercise, how is the breathing rate at rest?
questions.explanation: Compared with the breathing rate during exercise, the breathing rate at rest is lower.

questions.prompt: What percentage of oxygen does inspired air contain?
questions.explanation: Inspired air contains 21% oxygen.

questions.prompt: What percentage of oxygen does expired air contain?
questions.explanation: Expired air contains 16% oxygen.

questions.prompt: What percentage of carbon dioxide does inspired air contain?
questions.explanation: Inspired air contains 0.04% carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: What percentage of carbon dioxide does expired air contain?
questions.explanation: Expired air contains 4% carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: How are the water vapours in expired air?
questions.explanation: The water vapours in expired air are saturated.

questions.prompt: How are the water vapours in inspired air?
questions.explanation: The water vapours in inspired air are variable.

questions.prompt: What is the temperature of expired air?
questions.explanation: The temperature of expired air is 38 °C.

questions.prompt: How is the temperature of inspired air?
questions.explanation: The temperature of inspired air is variable.

questions.prompt: Compared with inspired air, how much oxygen does expired air contain?
questions.explanation: Compared with inspired air, expired air contains less oxygen.

questions.prompt: Compared with inspired air, how much carbon dioxide does expired air contain?
questions.explanation: Compared with inspired air, expired air contains more carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: How many times more carbon dioxide does expired air (4%) contain than inspired air (0.04%)?
questions.explanation: The carbon dioxide in expired air (4%) is 100 times that in inspired air (0.04%).

questions.prompt: By how much does the oxygen percentage fall from inspired air (21%) to expired air (16%)?
questions.explanation: The oxygen percentage falls by 5% from inspired air (21%) to expired air (16%).

questions.prompt: Tobacco smoke contains over how many different chemicals?
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains over 4,000 different chemicals.

questions.prompt: Tobacco smoke contains more than how many known carcinogens?
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains more than 69 known carcinogens.

questions.prompt: What are carcinogens?
questions.explanation: Carcinogens are cancer-causing chemicals.

questions.prompt: Smokers have a much higher risk of developing which kind of diseases?
questions.explanation: Smokers have a much higher risk of developing life-threatening diseases.

questions.prompt: Which substance makes up the majority of the particulate matter inhaled by a smoker?
questions.explanation: Tar makes up the majority of the particulate matter inhaled by a smoker.

questions.prompt: Tar stains the teeth and which other body part of smokers?
questions.explanation: Tar stains the teeth and fingers of smokers.

questions.prompt: Tar increases the production of which substance in the airways?
questions.explanation: Tar increases the production of mucus in the airways.

questions.prompt: What does tar contain many of?
questions.explanation: Tar contains many carcinogens.

questions.prompt: What does nicotine cause in the blood vessels?
questions.explanation: Nicotine causes constriction of the blood vessels.

questions.prompt: Nicotine increases which property of platelets in the blood, which can cause blockage?
questions.explanation: Nicotine increases platelet stickiness in the blood, which can cause blockage.

questions.prompt: The blockage caused by nicotine can lead to which diseases?
questions.explanation: The blockage caused by increased platelet stickiness can lead to coronary diseases.

questions.prompt: Besides disturbing hormonal systems and metabolism, nicotine damages the:
questions.explanation: Nicotine damages the muscles and disturbs the hormonal systems and metabolism.

questions.prompt: Nicotine disturbs the hormonal systems and which other body process?
questions.explanation: Nicotine disturbs the hormonal systems and metabolism.

questions.prompt: Nicotine increases the heart rate and which other measure of the circulatory system?
questions.explanation: Nicotine increases the heart rate and blood pressure.

questions.prompt: Which gas is formed when a cigarette is lit?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide is formed when a cigarette is lit.

questions.prompt: Carbon monoxide combines with which cells and prevents oxygen transportation?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide combines with red blood cells and prevents oxygen transportation.

questions.prompt: Carbon monoxide prevents the transportation of which gas?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide prevents the transportation of oxygen.

questions.prompt: Carbon monoxide and other toxic chemicals stay in the air ways and cause:
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide stays in the air ways along with other toxic chemicals, which cause inflammation.

questions.prompt: Which major component of cigarettes is a carcinogen that causes blood cancer?
questions.explanation: Benzene is a major component of cigarettes and is a carcinogen.

questions.prompt: What is blood cancer caused by benzene called?
questions.explanation: Benzene causes blood cancer, also called leukaemia.

questions.prompt: Which chemical in cigarettes causes cancers and respiratory, skin and gastrointestinal problems?
questions.explanation: Formaldehyde present in cigarettes causes cancers and respiratory, skin and gastrointestinal problems.

questions.prompt: Formaldehyde causes cancers and respiratory, skin and which other problems?
questions.explanation: Formaldehyde causes cancers and respiratory, skin and gastrointestinal problems.

questions.prompt: How many different metals are found in cigarette smoke?
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoke contains 30 different metals.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a metal found in cigarette smoke, along with arsenic, nickel, cadmium and chromium?
questions.explanation: Metals found in cigarette smoke include arsenic, nickel, cadmium, chromium and lead.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.8, cadmium found in cigarette smoke is also used in:
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoke contains cadmium, which is also used in batteries.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.8, arsenic found in cigarette smoke is also used as:
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoke contains arsenic, which is also used as a poison.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.8, nicotine found in cigarette smoke is also used as:
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoke contains nicotine, which is also used as an insecticide.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.8, methane found in cigarette smoke is also known as:
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoke contains methane, which is also known as sewer gas.

questions.prompt: In Fig. 10.8, toluene found in cigarette smoke is also used as an industrial:
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoke contains toluene, which is also used as an industrial solvent.
